formationLabel: Lithuanian Catholic society organized in 1916 · parish formed March 17, 1917 · later closed, exact terminal date unresolved
currentUse: The former St. George church at 369 Livingston Avenue survives as the Sister Maureen Joyce Center. A 2011 report identified the conversion and dedication, Lithuania's official 2024 U.S. heritage list identifies the former church and current center at the same address, and a 2024 All Saints bulletin documents continuing soup-kitchen service there. This is building continuity and charitable reuse, not continued parish life.
summary: St. George was Albany's Lithuanian Roman Catholic parish, formed from a Lithuanian Catholic society in 1917 and distinct from Utica's same-named Lithuanian parish. The parish worshiped at 369 Livingston Avenue and remained open at least into 1993, when a Black Apostolate helped sustain the church. It later closed on an unresolved date. The Diocese of Albany now directs St. George institutional records inquiries to St. Joan of Arc Church, while the former Livingston Avenue church serves as the Sister Maureen Joyce Center.

historicalNarrative.text: Albany's St. George grew from the Capital District's Lithuanian immigrant community, not from any St. George institution elsewhere in New York. A documented local history says Lithuanians formed St. George's Society in 1916 so they could receive Catholic ministry in their own language. The same source names Father Constantine F. Szatkus as the priest permitted to care for the community.

The local history dates the change from society to parish to March 17, 1917 and says a church was soon built on Livingston Avenue. This separates community organization in 1916 from parish formation in 1917. No reviewed public source in this tranche supplies the diocesan erection decree or a dedication date for the building.

The Livingston Avenue parish survived well beyond the inherited 1986 closure reading. The local history reports that only about twenty members remained in 1993, but Father Kofi Amissah persuaded Bishop Howard Hubbard to retain the church for an African-American apostolate. That pastoral broadening is not a new parish identity and does not establish the later terminal date.

The parish later closed, but the effective date and canonical mechanism remain unresolved. By October 2011 the former St. George church had been converted and dedicated as the Sister Maureen Joyce Center. The Diocese of Albany's current institutional-records directory separately routes St. George inquiries to St. Joan of Arc Church; that routing establishes records custody, not a merger or successor identity.

historicalNarrative.text: The building has a documented life separate from the closed institution. Lithuania's official 2024 list identifies St. George's former church, the Sister Maureen Joyce Center, and 369 Livingston Avenue as one heritage site. A December 2024 All Saints bulletin confirms continuing soup-kitchen service at that address. These sources support a standing converted building in charitable use, not surviving St. George parish worship.

conflictsWithArchiveRecord: The inherited 1986 terminal year is contradicted by the sourced account that St. George remained open in 1993 through an African-American apostolate. The reviewed evidence proves closure only within the wider interval after 1993 and before the former church's 2011 conversion dedication. Albany St. George is distinct from Utica St. George despite the shared patron and state.
gaps: The parish's exact canonical erection instrument; the church's construction and dedication dates; every possible earlier hosted-worship location; the effective closure date and decree; the relationship between parish closure and the Black Apostolate; completeness of records custody; any parish cemetery; and interior preservation after conversion remain unresolved.
